(FDR `r fmt_p(sig_mod$FDR[sig_mod$module == "Hep-M12"])`). Its highest-connectivity
members are *FGB*, *FGG*, *FGA*, *FGL1*, *CP*, *CYP3A5* and *PCK1*: fibrinogen
synthesis, copper transport, drug metabolism and gluconeogenesis. It is a
hepatocyte secretory and metabolic identity program, and it is the single
most-perturbed coordinated unit found anywhere in this analysis.

Two further observations: The upregulated
hepatocyte module Hep-M6 contains *PPARA*, *MLXIPL* and *PLIN5*, and the
upregulated stellate module HSC-M3 contains *NR1H4*. Both are nuclear receptors
with existing pharmacology in metabolic liver disease, which is a reassuring
sign that the signature is not disconnected from known biology. Nothing here directly
tests any drug, and no directional inference about a therapeutic effect follows
from a module changing.

# Discussion

## What this dataset can and cannot say about MASH therapeutics

MASH now has FDA approved drugs and a crowded development pipeline, and a natural
question is whether a dataset like this speaks to any of them. It does, but only
in a specific and limited way.

An observational cross-sectional cohort of 48 donors can establish two things
about a drug target: whether the target is expressed in the cell type the drug
is meant to act on, and whether the program that target controls is among the
things disease has perturbed. Those are questions about whether a mechanism is
*engageable* and *relevant* in human MASH liver. 

With that stated, the dataset does separate the pipeline into three groups.

```{r}
#| label: drug-targets

drug_expr <- cached("drug_target_expr.rds", {
  library(BPCells)
  mt <- open_matrix_dir("bpcells_counts")
  meta <- readRDS(cache_path("meta.rds"))
  k <- !meta[[COL_CT_BROAD]] %in% DROP_LABELS
  ctf <- factor(as.character(meta[[COL_CT_BROAD]])[k]); sb <- mt[, which(k)]
  nmz <- log1p(multiply_cols(sb, 1e4 / colSums(sb)))
  gg <- c("THRB","DIO1","GLP1R","GCGR","GIPR","KLB","FGFR1","NR1H4","NR0B2",
          "PPARA","PPARD","PPARG","ITGAV","ITGB1","ITGB6","ITGB8",
          "TGFB1","TGFBR1","TGFBR2","LOXL2","LOX","LOXL1")
  present <- gg[gg %in% rownames(mt)]
  a <- pseudobulk_matrix(nmz[present, ], cell_groups = ctf, method = "mean")
  n <- pseudobulk_matrix(sb[present, ],  cell_groups = ctf, method = "nonzeros")
  list(avg = a, pct = sweep(n, 2, as.integer(table(ctf)), "/") * 100,
       absent = setdiff(gg, present))
})

targ <- data.frame(
  Target = c("THRB", "GCGR", "GLP1R", "GIPR", "KLB", "NR1H4", "PPARA", "PPARD",
             "PPARG", "ITGAV", "ITGB6", "TGFB1", "LOXL2", "LOX"),
  Drug = c("resmetirom", "survodutide (glucagon arm)", "semaglutide",
           "tirzepatide (GIP arm)", "FGF21 analogues", "FXR agonists",
           "elafibranor, lanifibranor", "seladelpar, elafibranor",
           "lanifibranor", "integrin inhibitors", "integrin avb6 inhibitors",
           "TGF-beta blockade", "simtuzumab", "LOX inhibitors"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

look <- function(g, what) {
  if (g %in% drug_expr$absent) return(NA_real_)
  m <- drug_expr[[what]]
  if (!g %in% rownames(m)) return(NA_real_)
  max(m[g, ])
}
where <- function(g) {
  if (g %in% drug_expr$absent) return("not in object")
  colnames(drug_expr$avg)[which.max(drug_expr$avg[g, ])]
}
targ$`Highest in`  <- sapply(targ$Target, where)
targ$`Mean expr`   <- round(sapply(targ$Target, look, "avg"), 2)
targ$`% expressing`<- round(sapply(targ$Target, look, "pct"), 1)
kable(targ, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Where each target is expressed. Mean expression and percent are for the cell type where the target is highest.")
```

### Targets that are well represented in this tissue

**THR-beta (resmetirom).** *THRB* is expressed in
`r round(drug_expr$pct["THRB", "Hepatocyte"], 1)`% of hepatocytes, the highest of
any cell type, and it is not itself altered in disease. The programs it
regulates are hepatocyte fatty acid metabolism, bile acid metabolism and
xenobiotic metabolism are all significantly depleted in MASH here, and that loss
of differentiated metabolic function is the dominant hepatocyte finding in this
report. So the receptor is abundant and intact in exactly the cell type whose
metabolic program has degraded. That is a coherent target-tissue picture, and
it is the most straightforwardly supported mechanism in the dataset.

**FXR (obeticholic acid and successors).** *NR1H4* is well expressed in both
hepatocytes and stellate cells. More informative than the receptor is its
output: *NR0B2*, the canonical FXR target gene, is strongly reduced in
hepatocytes
(log2FC `r round(de$Hepatocyte$log2FoldChange[de$Hepatocyte$gene == "NR0B2"], 2)`,
FDR `r fmt_p(de$Hepatocyte$padj[de$Hepatocyte$gene == "NR0B2"])`), alongside the
depleted bile acid program. FXR signalling output is measurably lower in MASH
hepatocytes in this cohort. Whether restoring it is beneficial is a clinical
question this dataset cannot address, and the mixed clinical history of FXR
agonism is a reminder that pathway restoration and patient benefit are different
things.

**PPAR-alpha (elafibranor, lanifibranor).** *PPARA* is well expressed in
hepatocytes and unchanged in disease, and it sits inside `Hep-M6`, one of the
hepatocyte modules that moves significantly. *PPARG* is macrophage-biased, and
macrophages show the strongest cholesterol-homeostasis enrichment in the
dataset, which is at least consistent with a lipid-handling role for the
myeloid arm of a pan-PPAR agent. *PPARD* is poorly detected in every cell type
here, so this dataset can say little about selective delta agonism.

**Glucagon (survodutide's glucagon arm).** This one differs, and the distinction
is worth drawing. *GCGR* is expressed in
`r round(drug_expr$pct["GCGR", "Hepatocyte"], 1)`% of hepatocytes and is
modestly reduced in MASH
(log2FC `r round(de$Hepatocyte$log2FoldChange[de$Hepatocyte$gene == "GCGR"], 2)`,
FDR `r fmt_p(de$Hepatocyte$padj[de$Hepatocyte$gene == "GCGR"])`). Unlike the
GLP-1 and GIP components, the glucagon arm of a dual agonist has a direct
hepatocyte target that is measurable in this tissue. That makes glucagon-containing
dual agonists the incretin-class agents this dataset can actually say something
about.

### Targets whose liver action is not visible in this dataset

**GLP-1 (semaglutide).** *GLP1R* is not present in the object at all. This is not
a detection failure peculiar to this study: hepatocytes are not generally held to
express GLP-1 receptor, and the hepatic benefit of GLP-1 agonism is understood to
be largely indirect, through weight loss, glycaemic control and adipose
signalling. The consequence is simply that a liver transcriptomic atlas is the
wrong instrument for evaluating it. Its absence here is uninformative about the
drug.

**GIP (tirzepatide's GIP arm).** *GIPR* is effectively undetected in hepatocytes.
The same reasoning applies.

**FGF21 analogues.** The obligate co-receptor *KLB* is detected in only
`r round(drug_expr$pct["KLB", "Hepatocyte"], 1)`% of hepatocytes, and *FGFR1* is
essentially absent from hepatocytes while being present on stellate cells. FGF21
biology is substantially adipose-directed, so a liver dataset again under-reports
the mechanism.

### Anti-fibrotic targets: this dataset cannot evaluate them

```{r}
#| label: antifibrotic-targets

af <- c("LOX", "LOXL1", "LOXL2", "ITGB6", "ITGB1", "ITGAV", "TGFB1", "TGFBR1", "TGFBR2")
af <- af[!af %in% drug_expr$absent]
kable(data.frame(
  Target = af,
  `Highest in` = sapply(af, where),
  `Mean expr` = round(sapply(af, look, "avg"), 2),
  `% expressing` = round(sapply(af, look, "pct"), 1),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Anti-fibrotic drug targets, at the cell type where each is highest.")
```

The lysyl oxidases are the clearest case. *LOX* is essentially undetected,
*LOXL1* and *LOXL2* are detected in a few percent of stellate cells, and *LOXL2*
does not change significantly with disease. *ITGB6*, the target of alpha-v-beta-6
integrin inhibition, is effectively absent. *TGFB1* is low in every cell type,
and the TGF-beta signalling program is not significantly enriched in stellate
cells. Read naively, this would look like a dataset arguing against anti-fibrotic
targets.

That reading would be wrong, and the reason is documented earlier in this report.
These drugs act on collagen-producing myofibroblasts, and this dataset does not
contain them: the highest *COL1A1* count in any nucleus across the entire atlas
is
`r max(col1a1_counts())`, and the scar-associated
endothelial and mesenchymal populations from the reference cirrhosis atlas both
fail to appear while the scar-associated macrophage population replicates
cleanly. The most likely explanation for all of it is that needle-core
biopsy tissue does not recover cells resident in dense scar matrix.

So the correct statement is not that this dataset provides weak support for
anti-fibrotic mechanisms. It is that **this dataset cannot assess them**, because
the cell population those drugs target is missing from it for reasons of tissue
sampling rather than biology. An apparent absence of a drug target is only
evidence when the cells that would express it were recoverable in the first
place. The one anti-fibrotic-adjacent target that does move is *ITGAV* in
stellate cells
(log2FC `r round(de$Stellate_cell$log2FoldChange[de$Stellate_cell$gene == "ITGAV"], 2)`,
FDR `r fmt_p(de$Stellate_cell$padj[de$Stellate_cell$gene == "ITGAV"])`), which is
suggestive and no more.

### Does the data support combination therapy?

Not directly, and any dataset of this design would struggle to. What it does
provide is a structural argument, which is weaker but not empty.

The central result of this report is that MASH perturbation is distributed
across cell types along two independent axes, and that the axes do not coincide.
Hepatocytes lose a metabolic program and are depleted. Macrophages switch
identity from resident Kupffer to scar-associated without much change in number.
Endothelial cells carry the second-largest expression program in the dataset
with no abundance change at all, and its content is inflammatory. Lymphocytes
expand several-fold with comparatively little transcriptional change.

A hepatocyte-directed metabolic agent, whether a thyromimetic, an incretin or a
PPAR agonist, addresses the first of those compartments. Nothing in this data
suggests it would directly reach the macrophage identity switch or the
endothelial inflammatory program, both of which are large, statistically
robust and confined to cell types the metabolic targets are not expressed in.
That distribution is a reason to expect that a single-compartment intervention
leaves a substantial part of the measured disease untouched.

What this dataset cannot do is tell you which second agent to employ. Adjudicating a
metabolic-plus-anti-fibrotic combination specifically would require measuring
the fibrotic compartment, and this tissue preparation does not recover it (but at least we now know that). A
study built on precision-cut liver slices (like the kind I've done in the past at Pliant), resections or explants, where
myofibroblasts and the scar-resident niche are retained, is the design that
could potentially answer the direct anti-fibrotic question.

## Limitations

**Compositional dependence.** Proportions sum to one, so the loss of half the
hepatocyte compartment mechanically inflates every other fraction. The immune
expansions are relative enrichments. Distinguishing that from absolute
infiltration would require a cell-number-per-unit-tissue measurement that
dissociation-based data cannot provide.

**No batch variable.** The deposit carries no sequencing run, chemistry or
processing-date column, so no technical covariate could be tested or adjusted
for. The cohort is single-center, which limits the risk, but this cannot be
verified from what was deposited.

**Fibrosis is available only as a dichotomy.** The source study staged fibrosis
on the full Brunt/Kleiner F0-F4 scale, but used it only to define the eMASH
(F0-2) and aMASH (F3-4) groups, and the per-donor stage was not deposited. The
metadata carries disease group and nothing else clinical: no fibrosis stage, no
activity score, no ALT, and no age, sex or BMI. The finest fibrosis comparison
possible here is therefore the two-bin eMASH-versus-aMASH contrast, on 9 and 10
donors. No dose-response across F0 to F4 can be tested, and the stellate result
above should be read with that in mind: it is a difference between two coarse
fibrosis bins, not a gradient. The same constraint rules out relating cell-type
proportions to clinical severity, which the source paper was able to do because
it had the clinical table.

**Label heterogeneity is a real constraint.** The stellate result demonstrates
that pseudobulk over a mixed label can invert a program's apparent direction.
The same risk applies in principle to every label used here. It was caught in
this instance because the expected direction was known in advance and checked.

**Controls are not healthy volunteers.** They are biopsies from people
undergoing clinical procedures with no MASLD diagnosis. A baseline of stellate
activation and immune presence is expected, and comparisons are against that
baseline, not against normal liver.

**Unequal and modest group sizes.** The stage-resolved contrasts rest on 6 to 10
donors per arm. The eMASH-versus-aMASH stellate result does not survive
multiple-testing correction and is reported as suggestive for that reason.

**Reused integration and inherited annotation.** The analysis relies on the
deposited Liger integration and cluster labels rather than re-deriving them. That is deliberate: the labels
were validated against canonical markers before use, and re-clustering a
published, already-integrated object risks recapitulating the original result
rather than testing it. It does mean any error in the deposited annotation
propagates here, as the stellate `inactivated` subcluster illustrates. That case
also shows the check working: the mixture was detectable from marker expression,
from unbiased enrichment and from the subcluster-level profile, without
re-clustering anything.


# Supplementary

## Within-lineage resolution

Two lineages subdivide in the deposited annotation, and both subdivide along an
axis MASH acts on. This is where the detailed labels earn their place.

```{r}
#| label: detailed
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.6

sub_frac <- function(prefix) {
  s  <- md[grepl(prefix, md[[COL_CT_FINE]]), ]
  tb <- table(s[[COL_DONOR]], s[[COL_CT_FINE]])
  pr <- sweep(tb, 1, rowSums(tb), "/") * 100
  st <- donors$stage[match(rownames(pr), donors$donor)]
  data.frame(donor = rep(rownames(pr), ncol(pr)),
             subtype = rep(colnames(pr), each = nrow(pr)),
             pct = as.vector(pr), stage = rep(st, ncol(pr)))
}

st_frac  <- sub_frac("^Stellate")
hep_frac <- sub_frac("^Hepatocyte")

ggplot(rbind(st_frac, hep_frac), aes(stage, pct, fill = stage)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ subtype, nrow = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#4C72B0", "#DD8452", "#C44E52", "#8172B3")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "% of parent lineage") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

```{r}
#| label: detailed-table
sm <- function(d) round(sapply(levels(donors$stage), function(s)
  tapply(d$pct[d$stage == s], d$subtype[d$stage == s], mean, na.rm = TRUE)), 1)
kable(rbind(sm(st_frac), sm(hep_frac)),
      caption = "Mean composition within each lineage (%), by stage.")
```

Hepatocyte zonation shifts consistently: the pericentral fraction rises across
the progression while periportal and interzonal fractions fall. Given that
hepatocytes are simultaneously halving in absolute proportion, this is a
relative change in which zonal identity survives, not evidence that pericentral
hepatocytes increase in number.

The stellate substates move much less than their names suggest. The activated
fraction is already
`r round(mean(st_frac$pct[st_frac$subtype == "Stellate_cell_activated" & st_frac$stage == "No-MASLD"], na.rm = TRUE), 1)`%
in controls and reaches only
`r round(mean(st_frac$pct[st_frac$subtype == "Stellate_cell_activated" & st_frac$stage == "aMASH"], na.rm = TRUE), 1)`%
in advanced MASH. The controls are liver biopsies from people undergoing
clinical procedures rather than healthy volunteers, so a non-trivial baseline of
stellate activation is plausible.

The substate that does move sharply is `inactivated`, which falls from
`r round(mean(st_frac$pct[st_frac$subtype == "Stellate_cell_inactivated" & st_frac$stage == "No-MASLD"], na.rm = TRUE), 1)`%
to
`r round(mean(st_frac$pct[st_frac$subtype == "Stellate_cell_inactivated" & st_frac$stage == "aMASH"], na.rm = TRUE), 1)`%.
That turns out to matter more than the activated fraction, and it is taken up in
detail below, after the enrichment results supply a second line of evidence
about what that subcluster actually contains.

How these substate labels were produced is relevant to reading them. The source
paper's supplementary methods describe subclustering all donors together, then
subclustering disease and control cells separately, and assigning a substate
only where both analyses agreed. Cells that disagreed were labeled
`Unidentified`, and subclusters showing ectopic marker expression were labeled
`misc`. That is a conservative procedure, but it means the substate assignments
are not independent of disease status, so substate proportions compared across
disease groups should be read as descriptive rather than as a clean test.


## Is this a technical gradient?

Enrichment on pseudobulk is vulnerable to a specific failure: proliferation and
biosynthesis sets are loaded with highly expressed housekeeping genes, so a
systematic difference in capture depth between groups can produce a sweep of
significant hits that reflect nothing biological. Three checks decide whether
that is happening here.

```{r}
#| label: gsea-diagnostic

sig <- subset(gs_all, padj < 0.05)
spread <- aggregate(NES ~ pathway, sig, function(x) c(n = length(x), lo = min(x), hi = max(x)))
spread <- data.frame(pathway = spread$pathway, n_types = spread$NES[, "n"],
                     NES_min = round(spread$NES[, "lo"], 2),
                     NES_max = round(spread$NES[, "hi"], 2))
spread <- spread[order(-spread$n_types), ][1:6, ]

pb_sel <- pbmeta$n_cells >= MIN_CELLS & !is.na(pbmeta$condition)
depth  <- tapply(colSums(pb[, pbmeta$pseudosample[pb_sel]]) /
                 pbmeta$n_cells[pb_sel], pbmeta$condition[pb_sel], median)

kable(spread, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Pathways significant in the most cell types, with the range of their enrichment scores.")
```

**The most widely significant pathways change sign between cell types.**
`MYC_TARGETS_V1` runs from NES `r round(min(subset(sig, pathway == "MYC_TARGETS_V1")$NES), 2)`
to `r round(max(subset(sig, pathway == "MYC_TARGETS_V1")$NES), 2)` depending on
which cell type is examined. A depth artifact would push every cell type in the
same direction.

**Median counts per nucleus are comparable between groups**
(`r round(depth[["Control"]])` in Control, `r round(depth[["MASH"]])` in MASH),
and DESeq2 models library size explicitly in any case.

**The leading-edge genes are process-specific, not housekeeping.** The strongest
single result in the dataset is loss of `E2F_TARGETS` in NK cells, and its
leading edge is *RRM2*, *MELK*, *BIRC5*, *MCM4*, *MCM6*, *ORC6*, *CENPE*:
replication and mitotic machinery, with no ribosomal protein genes at all.

The results are therefore read as biological.

## Localizing the mixture to one subcluster

The annotation section established that the subcluster labeled
`Stellate_cell_inactivated` is vascular mural rather than stellate. This section
works out what that mislabel does to the aggregate stellate results, which is
where it matters.

One point of context first. The source paper defines its *inactivated* state on
*PDGFRB*, *TAGLN*, *ACTA2* and *PPARG*, so *ACTA2* and *TAGLN* are markers of
that state rather than of activation. Loss of those genes from the stellate
compartment therefore has two candidate explanations, mural contamination or
genuine loss of an inactivated stellate population, and they are separable
because they predict different behavior from smooth-muscle genes that appear in
neither panel.

```{r}
#| label: stellate-subtypes

sub_expr <- cached("stellate_subtype_expr.rds", {
  library(BPCells)
  mat  <- open_matrix_dir("bpcells_counts")
  meta <- readRDS(cache_path("meta.rds"))
  sel  <- grepl("^Stellate", meta[[COL_CT_FINE]])
  ctf  <- factor(as.character(meta[[COL_CT_FINE]])[sel])
  sb   <- mat[, which(sel)]
  nm   <- log1p(multiply_cols(sb, 1e4 / colSums(sb)))
  g <- c("DCN", "RBP1", "LRAT", "CYGB", "HGF", "COL1A1", "COL1A2",
         "PDGFRB", "TAGLN", "ACTA2", "PPARG",
         "MYH11", "MYLK", "MYL9", "NOTCH3", "RGS5")
  g <- g[g %in% rownames(mat)]
  t(pseudobulk_matrix(nm[g, ], cell_groups = ctf, method = "mean"))
})

rownames(sub_expr) <- sub("Stellate_cell_", "", rownames(sub_expr))
kable(round(sub_expr[, c("LRAT", "DCN", "RBP1", "COL1A1",
                         "ACTA2", "TAGLN", "PDGFRB",
                         "MYH11", "NOTCH3", "RGS5")], 2),
      caption = "Mean log-normalized expression by stellate subcluster. Left block: hepatic stellate identity. Middle: the paper's inactivated-state panel. Right: smooth-muscle and pericyte genes used by neither panel.")
```

The inactivated subcluster carries
`r round(sub_expr["inactivated", "MYH11"] / max(sub_expr[rownames(sub_expr) != "inactivated", "MYH11"]))`-fold
more *MYH11* than any other stellate subcluster, along with the only appreciable
*NOTCH3*, while showing the **lowest** *LRAT* and *DCN* of the four.

That combination decides the question. *MYH11* is smooth-muscle myosin heavy
chain and is not expressed by hepatic stellate cells in any activation state. A
genuinely inactivated stellate cell, one that has reverted after activation,
retains its lipid-storing identity markers; this population has the least *LRAT*
and *DCN* of any subcluster while uniquely expressing *MYH11* and *NOTCH3*. It
is better described as vascular smooth muscle or pericyte than as a stellate
cell of any state.

That mural population also declines across the progression, falling from
`r round(mean(st_frac$pct[st_frac$subtype == "Stellate_cell_inactivated" & st_frac$stage == "No-MASLD"], na.rm = TRUE), 1)`%
to
`r round(mean(st_frac$pct[st_frac$subtype == "Stellate_cell_inactivated" & st_frac$stage == "aMASH"], na.rm = TRUE), 1)`%
of the compartment, which is the right shape to inflate an apparent loss of
contractile genes when the whole label is aggregated.

### How much of the effect is composition?

The tempting conclusion is that the entire contractile signal is a mixture
artifact. That is testable in two ways, and the test does not fully support it.

```{r}
#| label: stellate-decompose

# 1. Rebuild the stellate pseudobulk with the mural subcluster removed.
# 2. Test inside single subtypes, where composition is fixed by construction and
#    any remaining change must be a within-cell-type effect.
decomp <- cached("stellate_decompose.rds", {
  library(BPCells); library(DESeq2)
  meta <- readRDS(cache_path("meta.rds")); mt <- open_matrix_dir("bpcells_counts")
  dn <- unique(meta[, c(COL_DONOR, COL_STAGE)])
  cnd <- setNames(unname(CONDITION_MAP[dn[[COL_STAGE]]]), dn[[COL_DONOR]])

  de_on <- function(subtypes) {
    sel <- meta[[COL_CT_FINE]] %in% subtypes
    grp <- paste0("g__", meta[[COL_DONOR]][sel])
    p <- pseudobulk_matrix(mt[, which(sel)], cell_groups = grp, method = "sum")
    n <- table(grp)[colnames(p)]; dono <- sub("g__", "", colnames(p))
    keep <- n >= MIN_CELLS & !is.na(cnd[dono])
    cts <- round(p[, keep, drop = FALSE]); mode(cts) <- "integer"
    cts <- cts[rowSums(cts > 0) >= ceiling(ncol(cts) / 3), , drop = FALSE]
    cd <- data.frame(condition = factor(cnd[dono[keep]], levels = CONDITION_LEVELS),
                     row.names = colnames(cts))
    dds <- DESeq(DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(cts, cd, ~ condition), quiet = TRUE)
    r <- as.data.frame(results(dds, contrast = c("condition", "MASH", "Control")))
    r$gene <- rownames(r); r$n_control <- sum(cd$condition == "Control")
    r$n_mash <- sum(cd$condition == "MASH"); r
  }
  list(
    hsc_only  = de_on(c("Stellate_cell_quiescent", "Stellate_cell_activated",
                        "Stellate_cell_misc")),
    quiescent = de_on("Stellate_cell_quiescent"),
    activated = de_on("Stellate_cell_activated"))
})

pull <- function(r, g) {
  i <- match(g, r$gene)
  sprintf("%+.2f%s", r$log2FoldChange[i],
          ifelse(is_de(r)[i], "*", ""))
}
gg <- c("TAGLN", "ACTA2", "MYH11", "MYL9", "LRAT", "COL1A1", "COL3A1")
kable(data.frame(
  Gene = gg,
  `All stellate` = pull(de$Stellate_cell, gg),
  `Mural removed` = pull(decomp$hsc_only, gg),
  `Quiescent only` = pull(decomp$quiescent, gg),
  `Activated only` = pull(decomp$activated, gg),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = paste0("log2 fold change, MASH vs Control, as the mural subcluster is ",
                   "removed and then as the test is confined within single subtypes. * = ", DE_RULE, "."))
```

The two contractile genes behave differently, and the distinction matters.

*MYH11* loses significance as soon as the mural subcluster is removed and stays
non-significant inside both subtypes. That is what a pure composition effect
looks like, and it confirms the mural reading.

*TAGLN* does not. It remains strongly depleted inside the quiescent subcluster
and inside the activated subcluster, tested separately, where composition is
fixed by construction and cannot contribute. That is a real transcriptional
change within hepatic stellate cells.

So both mechanisms are operating, and an earlier reading of this result as
purely a mixture artifact would have been wrong. A mural population is inflating
the aggregate signal, which is why `MYOGENESIS` weakens from
`r round(subset(gs_all, cell_type == "Stellate_cell" & pathway == "MYOGENESIS")$NES, 2)`
to non-significance once those cells are excluded. Underneath it there is a
genuine, subtype-independent downregulation of *TAGLN* in stellate cells. What
the data do not support is the simple statement that stellate cells are losing
their activation program wholesale: *LRAT* rises rather than falls, and the
fibrillar collagens do not move significantly in either direction. That last
point should not be read as evidence against fibrogenesis either: as quantified
in the limitations, this dataset contains no collagen-producing myofibroblast
population to detect a change in.

This remains a caution about the deposited annotation, and it is only visible
because the deposit ships substate labels alongside the broad ones. It is also a
concrete illustration of the general hazard, with the qualification that
decomposing the effect matters: pseudobulk over a mixed label can exaggerate a
program, and separating composition from within-cell-type change requires
testing at a level where composition cannot vary.

## Comparison with the source paper's own enrichment

The source paper ran its own enrichment on the same tissue, reported in its
Supplementary Table 3. Comparing against it tests whether the pathway-level
conclusions here depend on the analytical choices made in this report.

Four differences matter when reading the comparison. Their differential
expression was cell-level Seurat `FindMarkers`, against donor-level pseudobulk
here. Their enrichment was over-representation testing with enrichR on
thresholded gene lists, against GSEA on the full ranking here. Their gene sets
were GO Biological Process, against Hallmark here, and the two collections do
not map one-to-one. And their comparison pooled MASL into the reference group as
"nonMASH", where the primary contrast here holds MASL out. Their table also
reports only the top four terms in each direction, so a term missing from it is
not evidence that they found nothing.

```{r}
#| label: paper-comparison

# Terms as reported in Hong et al. Supplementary Table 3 (GO Biological Process,
# enrichR, MASH vs nonMASH). Quoted here as reference values; every value in the
# "this report" columns is computed from the GSEA above.
paper <- data.frame(
  cell_type = c("Hepatocyte", "Hepatocyte", "Hepatocyte", "Hepatocyte",
                "Cholangiocyte", "Cholangiocyte", "Cholangiocyte",
                "Stellate_cell", "Stellate_cell",
                "Endothelial_cell", "Endothelial_cell"),
  paper_term = c("cholesterol biosynthetic process", "steroid metabolic process",
                 "drug catabolic process", "cellular amino acid catabolic process",
                 "mitochondrial electron transport", "Notch signaling pathway",
                 "regulation of canonical Wnt signaling",
                 "muscle contraction", "collagen fibril organization",
                 "cellular response to interferon-gamma",
                 "positive regulation of cell migration"),
  paper_dir = c("up", "down", "down", "down",
                "down", "up", "up",
                "down", "up",
                "down", "up"),
  hallmark = c("CHOLESTEROL_HOMEOSTASIS", "BILE_ACID_METABOLISM",
               "XENOBIOTIC_METABOLISM", "FATTY_ACID_METABOLISM",
               "OXIDATIVE_PHOSPHORYLATION", "NOTCH_SIGNALING",
               "WNT_BETA_CATENIN_SIGNALING",
               "MYOGENESIS", "EPITHELIAL_MESENCHYMAL_TRANSITION",
               "INTERFERON_GAMMA_RESPONSE", "EPITHELIAL_MESENCHYMAL_TRANSITION"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

lookup <- function(ct, pw, field) {
  r <- gs_all[gs_all$cell_type == ct & gs_all$pathway == pw, ]
  if (!nrow(r)) return(NA_real_)
  r[[field]][1]
}
paper$NES <- mapply(lookup, paper$cell_type, paper$hallmark, "NES")
paper$FDR <- mapply(lookup, paper$cell_type, paper$hallmark, "padj")
paper$this_dir <- ifelse(is.na(paper$NES), NA,
                  ifelse(paper$FDR >= 0.05, "n.s.",
                  ifelse(paper$NES > 0, "up", "down")))
paper$agrees <- ifelse(paper$this_dir == "n.s.", "not significant",
                ifelse(paper$this_dir == paper$paper_dir, "agrees", "opposite"))

kable(data.frame(
  `Cell type` = paper$cell_type,
  `Paper GO term` = paper$paper_term,
  `Paper` = paper$paper_dir,
  `Matched Hallmark set` = paper$hallmark,
  `NES` = round(paper$NES, 2),
  `FDR` = signif(paper$FDR, 2),
  `Verdict` = paper$agrees,
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Terms reported in Hong et al. Supplementary Table 3, against the nearest Hallmark set in this analysis.")
```

**Hepatocyte metabolic reprogramming replicates completely.** All four reported
directions agree: cholesterol handling up, and steroid, drug-catabolic and
fatty-acid metabolism down. Two methods that share nothing except the underlying
tissue reach the same conclusion, which is the strongest form of corroboration
available here.

**Their table contains the stellate result independently.** Supplementary Table 3
reports *muscle contraction* as significantly depleted in stellate cells in
MASH. That is the same signal as the `MYOGENESIS` depletion above
(NES `r round(subset(gs_all, cell_type == "Stellate_cell" & pathway == "MYOGENESIS")$NES, 2)`),
recovered from different data processing, a different differential expression
method and a different gene set collection.

This matters for how the mural-cell interpretation should be read. The
observation is not particular to this pipeline: it is present in the source
paper's own supplementary results, where it is reported without interpretation.
What this report adds is the explanation, that the depletion reflects loss of a
mural population carried inside the stellate label rather than a change in
stellate contractile state.

### Where the two analyses diverge

```{r}
#| label: paper-grouping

# Their reference group pools MASL with controls. Rerunning the four cell types
# their table covers under that definition separates disagreements caused by the
# grouping from disagreements caused by method.
gsea_pooled <- cached("gsea_pooled.rds", {
  library(fgsea); library(msigdbr)
  hall <- msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "H")
  sets <- split(hall$gene_symbol, hall$gs_name)
  names(sets) <- sub("^HALLMARK_", "", names(sets))
  pm <- pbmeta
  pm$grp <- ifelse(pm$stage %in% c("No-MASLD", "MASL"), "nonMASH",
            ifelse(pm$stage %in% c("eMASH", "aMASH"), "MASH", NA))
  out <- list()
  for (ct in c("Hepatocyte", "Cholangiocyte", "Stellate_cell", "Endothelial_cell")) {
    sel <- pm$cell_type == ct & pm$n_cells >= MIN_CELLS & !is.na(pm$grp)
    m <- pm[sel, ]; m$grp <- factor(m$grp, levels = c("nonMASH", "MASH"))
    cts <- round(pb[, m$pseudosample, drop = FALSE]); mode(cts) <- "integer"
    cts <- cts[rowSums(cts > 0) >= ceiling(ncol(cts) / 3), , drop = FALSE]
    dds <- DESeq(DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(cts, m, ~ grp), quiet = TRUE)
    r <- as.data.frame(results(dds, contrast = c("grp", "MASH", "nonMASH")))
    r$gene <- rownames(r); r <- r[!is.na(r$stat), ]
    st <- setNames(r$stat, r$gene); st <- st[!duplicated(names(st))]
    set.seed(42)
    out[[ct]] <- as.data.frame(fgsea(sets, st, minSize = 10, maxSize = 500,
                                     nPermSimple = 10000))
  }
  out
})

pooled_get <- function(ct, pw) {
  r <- gsea_pooled[[ct]][gsea_pooled[[ct]]$pathway == pw, ]
  if (!nrow(r)) return(c(NA, NA))
  c(r$NES[1], r$padj[1])
}
diverge <- data.frame(
  `Cell type` = c("Stellate_cell", "Endothelial_cell", "Cholangiocyte", "Cholangiocyte"),
  `Hallmark set` = c("EPITHELIAL_MESENCHYMAL_TRANSITION", "INTERFERON_GAMMA_RESPONSE",
                     "NOTCH_SIGNALING", "WNT_BETA_CATENIN_SIGNALING"),
  check.names = FALSE)
mine <- t(mapply(function(ct, pw) c(lookup(ct, pw, "NES"), lookup(ct, pw, "padj")),
                 diverge$`Cell type`, diverge$`Hallmark set`))
pool <- t(mapply(pooled_get, diverge$`Cell type`, diverge$`Hallmark set`))
diverge$`NES (MASL held out)`   <- round(mine[, 1], 2)
diverge$`FDR (held out)`        <- signif(mine[, 2], 2)
diverge$`NES (MASL pooled in)`  <- round(pool[, 1], 2)
diverge$`FDR (pooled in)`       <- signif(pool[, 2], 2)
kable(diverge, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "The four disagreements, evaluated under both reference-group definitions.")
```

**One disagreement is entirely explained by the grouping.** The paper reports
collagen fibril organization up in stellate cells. Holding MASL out, the nearest
Hallmark set is not significant; pooling MASL into the reference as they did, it
becomes significantly up. The reason is visible in the composition data above:
MASL donors carry an unusually quiescent stellate compartment
(`r round(mean(st_frac$pct[st_frac$subtype == "Stellate_cell_quiescent" & st_frac$stage == "MASL"], na.rm = TRUE))`%
quiescent, against
`r round(mean(st_frac$pct[st_frac$subtype == "Stellate_cell_quiescent" & st_frac$stage == "No-MASLD"], na.rm = TRUE))`%
in controls), so folding them into the reference lowers its fibrogenic baseline
and widens the contrast. Both results are defensible; they answer slightly
different questions, and the fibrogenesis signal is worth knowing is sensitive
to that choice.

**One disagreement is not.** The paper reports the interferon-gamma response
down in endothelial cells; here it is up, under both reference definitions. The
leading edge is *VCAM1*, *CD274*, *IDO1*, *FAS* and *IL18BP*, which are
interferon-inducible endothelial activation genes, and *VCAM1* induction is
consistent with the leukocyte recruitment implied by the abundance results. The
direction is also coherent across the tissue: interferon-gamma response is up in
the structural compartments and down in every immune population tested. The most
likely source of the discrepancy is that Hallmark's response signature is broad
where the GO term is a narrower signalling set, compounded by cell-level versus
donor-level differential expression. This is flagged rather than resolved.

**Two of their findings are not reproduced.** Notch and Wnt signalling in
cholangiocytes are not significant here under either grouping. Cholangiocytes
are the least powered cell type in this analysis, with the fewest donors
clearing the pseudo-sample threshold, so this is weak evidence against their
result. Their Notch claim also rests primarily on cell-cell interaction
analysis, which is not attempted here.
